description: Applying one overlay. 'facts' describe the consumer: os, root, identity, state (its state directory), pinned, grants (what this overlay may read, by provider: secret names, file keys, host variables), base_env (the environment being built), host_env (its own), secrets (named), secret_files (the secrets directory), files (the overlay's files by relative path, with the text of those read as env files; the fields a manifest does not write take their defaults from them), providers, interpreters (the interpreters the consumer can run here; absent, python, node, powershell, bash and sh), env_scripts_enabled (the consumer's policy; absent, true), enforces_network, packages (each runtime's installed packages directory), and for setup phases change ('add', 'sync', 'activate' or 'remove'), digest (the overlay's), record (the digest and phase of the last preparation of this overlay that succeeded on this OS; absent, none) and fails (the step that fails: 'deps' or 'setup'). 'expect' gives the resulting environment, the selected setup and runtime variants, the dependencies (runtime, file, lock or null, environment), what a probe needs, and the weakenings as [id, subject], and with a change the setup_phase (null when nothing runs), setup_arguments (the phase, then the variant's args; null when no setup runs), the steps in order ('empty-state', 'deps:<runtime>', 'setup', 'record', 'delete'), the record afterwards, and whether the digest activates; or the refusal.

cases.description: No manifest: only the root variable; unpinned is reported.
Env files, env and paths in order on Linux; host and named secrets resolve.
The same overlay on Windows: the windows env file applies, ';' and '\', names without case.
Nothing granted: an optional reference stays unset and is listed; the host value is never read.
A required reference that is not granted cannot be resolved.
Optional references that cannot be resolved leave the variable unset.
A reference that cannot be resolved refuses, naming the variable.
A provider the consumer does not have cannot be resolved.
The file provider removes one trailing line feed.
A file key that is not a relative path is refused.
With no secrets directory a file reference cannot be resolved.
An empty value is a value: if_unset keeps it.
Setting a sensitive variable through env is reported; a path addition to PATH or PYTHONPATH is not.
A path addition to any other sensitive variable is reported.
An env file cannot set a reserved variable.
An env file cannot set a variable the overlay's paths name.
Prepends in order, existing components without duplicates or empties, appends in order; a repeated entry counts once.
The first variant whose os matches; defaults filled in; network and no timeout reported.
No network declared, and the consumer cannot deny it.
With a state directory, its variable is set beside the root's.
No variant matches: no setup on this OS.
Runtime variant selection, needs and unlocked dependencies.
An OS outside runtime.os.
A consumer whose own policy turns env scripts off runs none; nothing is reported or needed.
Enabled: each script for this OS, with defaults, reported.
MCP servers that read the host environment and secrets: granted ones are reported, the rest listed as not granted; plain http to a remote host is reported.
A listed env file that does not exist.
An env file whose values are not env values.
An env file that does not read as its format.
An aos env file names its own format.
No manifest and a bin/: bin/ goes first on PATH, and nothing else happens.
bin/ prepended to PATH, then lib/python/ prepended to PYTHONPATH.
The same on Windows: the existing Path keeps its name.
Not present: no file under bin/ or lib/python/ (a file named bin.txt, an excluded name, Bin/ in another case, a bare lib/).
[defaults] bin = false and lib = false turn both off.
Only bin off: lib/python/ still goes on PYTHONPATH.
Declared entries add to the defaults: bin/ stays first on PATH; the entry naming lib/python replaces that default and appends it, once; MANPATH is added.
A declared entry naming bin replaces the default even where its os does not apply.
A bin/ under the default: env cannot also set PATH.
With bin off, env may set PATH (a sensitive variable, reported).

A root file named env is read as dotenv: ${NAME} placeholders are substituted, single-quoted values and $(...) are characters, nothing runs; the overlay's own AOS_OVERLAY_ROOT and AOS_OVERLAY_NAME are seen, not set.
PATH=${MYTOOL_HOME}/bin:${PATH} on the line after MYTOOL_HOME: each line sees the earlier ones, and PATH its own earlier value.
Entries of one mapping see the environment before it, never each other (mapping order carries no meaning); env sees the env files.
A name the mapping itself sets, unset before it, is undefined: an error naming the variable being set.
Text in an aos env file is substituted, in both forms; a path is not.
A dotenv line cannot read a variable an earlier env file took from a secret reference.
The state directory is seen as AOS_OVERLAY_STATE and as the overlay's own state variable.
Without a state directory AOS_OVERLAY_STATE is undefined.
On Windows a placeholder finds Path as ${PATH}.
The default env file must read as dotenv.
The default env file cannot set a variable a default path addition names.
[defaults] env = false turns it off.
A declared env file is read after the default one.
A declared entry naming env replaces the default entry: here it applies on Windows only.
Several env.<ext>: the first in the order that can run, here env.py; one runs, reported.
No Python: the next that applies on Linux and has its interpreter, env.sh (env.ps1 applies on Windows only).
On Windows a shell script does not apply: env.ps1.
Node.js before the shells; .js before .mjs.
Present but none can run here: nothing runs, each file is reported, and the environment is still built.
[defaults] env_scripts = false turns it off.
A declared env script runs after the default one.
A declared entry naming env.py replaces the default entry with its own arguments and timeout; it runs once.
The configured env.py keeps its place in the order: without Python, env.sh is chosen and the configured entry does not run.
With the default off, a declared env.sh is an ordinary declared script.
A consumer whose policy turns env scripts off runs no default one either.
setup.<ext> chosen like an env script; a default setup needs the network (reported) and has the 300-second timeout.
On Windows, setup.ps1.
Present but none can run here: no setup, each file reported.
[defaults] setup = false turns it off.
To deny the default setup the network, declare an entry naming it: network then defaults to false.
Configuring setup.sh does not move it up the order: setup.py, still a default, is chosen and needs the network.
A declared variant that applies comes before the default setup.
No declared variant applies on Windows: the default setup is the last variant.
First add, nothing recorded: the state directory is made empty, setup runs install, and the digest and phase are recorded.
An add of an overlay already prepared under this identity is a sync.
A sync to a new digest: sync, the phase before the declared arguments.
Every sync runs setup, also when the digest did not change; the user asking to run setup again is such a sync.
A sync with nothing recorded (the earlier digest had nothing to prepare, or its install failed): install.
A consumer with no sync of its own, before it activates a digest other than the recorded one: sync.
Activating the recorded digest outside a sync: nothing runs.
Activating with nothing recorded: install.
Removing after a preparation that succeeded: remove, with the variant's own timeout and network, then the state directory, the record and the overlay's dependencies are deleted.
Removing with nothing recorded: setup does not run; the state directory is still deleted.
A failed remove: reported, and everything is deleted anyway.
A failed install: nothing is recorded and the overlay is not activated.
A failed sync to a new digest: the record still names the previous digest, and the new one is not activated.
A failed sync of the recorded digest: the record stands, so that digest stays active; the failure is reported.
Nothing to prepare on this OS (no setup, no dependencies): no phase runs.
Dependencies and no setup: the phase still applies; dependencies install and the record is kept, with no script to tell.
Dependencies install before setup runs, Python then Node.js, so setup can use them.
A failed dependency install stops the sync before setup; the previous record stands.
lib/python/requirements.txt installs into the shared Python environment, whose packages follow lib/python/ on PYTHONPATH; unhashed, it is reported unlocked, and installing needs the network.
A hash on every requirement makes the file a lock: no unlocked weakening; the network is still reported.
Hashes on some requirements and not others: refused.
lib/node/package.json with a package-lock.json beside it: installed with npm ci into the shared node_modules, on NODE_PATH after lib/node/; needs node and npm.
No package-lock.json: npm install, reported unlocked.
No dependency file in its place: nothing installs. A requirements.txt at the root or a node_modules/ has no meaning.
[defaults] deps = false: nothing installs; lib/python/ stays on PYTHONPATH.
A declared runtime.python lock replaces the default file.
A declared requirements file replaces it too, and is reported unlocked.
runtime.node package names another package.json; its package-lock.json beside it pins it.
A variant that names no file chooses the environment of the default one: isolated, the overlay's own.
A named environment, compared normalized.
On Windows, ';' separates PYTHONPATH and NODE_PATH as any list variable.
No other name has a default: requirements.txt, pre.env, pre.env.py, local.env, cmds/, an env/ directory, setup/setup.sh, env.cfg, a bare lib/; bin/tool.py is a program on PATH, not a command.
